flashcards.q: Define calibration precisely and distinguish it from discrimination/ranking (AUC).
flashcards.a: Calibrated: among predictions of probability p, the true outcome rate is ~p. AUC only measures whether positives rank above negatives across thresholds -- a model can have perfect AUC-ROC while being badly miscalibrated (wrong magnitudes, right order).

flashcards.q: Why can't recalibration (Platt/isotonic) change a model's AUC-ROC?
flashcards.a: Both are monotonic transformations of the raw score, and a monotonic transform cannot change the ranking of examples -- only the numeric probability values. AUC-ROC is purely rank-based, so it's unaffected by any monotonic recalibration.

flashcards.q: Platt scaling formula and its failure mode?
flashcards.a: p = 1/(1+exp(A*f+B)), 2 params fit by MLE on a held-out calibration set. Fails if the true miscalibration isn't sigmoid-shaped; needs little calibration data.

flashcards.q: Isotonic regression mechanism (pool-adjacent-violators) and its failure mode?
flashcards.a: Fits an arbitrary monotonic step function: merge adjacent blocks that violate ordering, average, repeat until fully monotonic. Corrects any miscalibration shape but needs more calibration data or it overfits (jagged, unreliable mapping).

flashcards.q: Why does accuracy fail on imbalanced data, with numbers?
flashcards.a: 1,000 positives / 99,000 negatives: predicting all-negative gets 99% accuracy while catching zero true positives -- a useless model outscores useful ones on this metric.

flashcards.q: Why does AUC-ROC 'lie' under class imbalance -- the mechanism?
flashcards.a: FPR = FP/(FP+TN) is normalized by the huge negative class, so a large absolute false-positive count looks like a tiny FPR. Same false positives compared against a small true-positive count tank precision (e.g. 2000 FP vs 800 TP -> 28.6% precision) -- a failure AUC-ROC hides but AUC-PR reveals.

flashcards.q: AUC-PR's random-classifier baseline, and why that matters for comparing across datasets?
flashcards.a: A random classifier's AUC-PR equals the positive class prevalence (not a fixed 0.5 like AUC-ROC). AUC-PR values aren't directly comparable across datasets with different base rates without accounting for this.

flashcards.q: Brier score formula and what makes it different from accuracy or AUC alone?
flashcards.a: mean((p-y)^2). Decomposes into calibration + refinement (discrimination) terms, jointly penalizing both bad ranking and bad calibration -- unlike accuracy or AUC, which each capture only one property.

flashcards.q: Cost-sensitive threshold formula and its hidden requirement?
flashcards.a: Flag positive when p*cost_FN > (1-p)*cost_FP, i.e. threshold p* = cost_FP/(cost_FP+cost_FN). Requires the model's probabilities to actually be calibrated -- an uncalibrated p makes this derived threshold meaningless.

flashcards.q: Why calibrate on a held-out set separate from the base model's training data?
flashcards.a: A model's scores on its own training data are systematically overconfident (partial memorization), so calibrating on them fits the mapping to that overconfidence rather than true out-of-sample behavior -- production data behaves like held-out data, not training data.
